q: Does CS-VQE extend cleanly to open-shell molecules (spin doublets/triplets, e.g. OH, O2, CH3) where the Hartree-Fock reference is no longer a single closed-shell determinant, and does the noncontextual partition still capture the dominant static correlation?
basis: The paper (and this replication) only test closed-shell singlets in minimal basis (H2, LiH, H2O, N2). Open-shell systems break the |1100>-style HF reference and typically require multi-configurational treatments; the noncontextual subspace is derived from a classical quasi-quantized model whose accuracy for radicals is unproven. Rick's candidate-probe list explicitly flags this as an open direction.
next_steps: (1) Build the STO-3G JW Hamiltonian for OH (7 electrons, 12 spin-orbitals -> 12 qubits) using OpenFermion+PySCF with ROHF or UHF as the reference. (2) Exhaustively (or, if intractable, greedily) enumerate noncontextual partitions and record the minimum q needed to reach 1 mHa of ROHF-CISD. (3) Compare CS-VQE qubit-reduction ratio for OH vs the paper's H2O row. (4) Repeat for O2 triplet as a stronger test of the quasi-quantized value assignment on a degenerate ground manifold.

q: How does CS-VQE compose with modern qubit-reduction techniques -- specifically Z2 symmetry tapering (Bravyi et al. 2017) and point-group symmetry reduction -- when applied sequentially, and are the reductions additive or does the noncontextual partition already absorb the same symmetries?
basis: Both tapering and CS-VQE reduce qubit count by finding stabilizer subgroups; if the noncontextual set already contains the Z2 taperable generators, sequential application would be redundant. The paper does not test the composition, and no downstream literature (as of 2026) has systematically benchmarked (taper -> CS) vs (CS -> taper) vs joint search.
next_steps: (1) For H2O/STO-3G (14 qubits pre-taper), run Qiskit-Nature's Z2Symmetries.find_z2_symmetries to identify N_up, N_dn, and reflection generators. (2) Measure the qubit count after (a) tapering alone, (b) CS-VQE alone with exhaustive partition search up to q=6, (c) taper-then-CS, (d) CS-then-taper. (3) Compare total qubit budget and total measurement cost to reach 1 mHa vs FCI. (4) Formally check whether the noncontextual generators produced by our greedy search intersect the Z2 taper generators (they should for trivially symmetric partitions).

q: Does CS-VQE remain useful for strongly-correlated systems (Cr2, stretched N2, transition-metal dimers) where the noncontextual approximation is expected to fail because multiple determinants have comparable weight, or does it degrade to full VQE (q -> n) as static correlation grows?
basis: The paper's H2 sweep at bond length 0.7414 Angstrom is in the weakly-correlated regime; near dissociation (H2 at 3.0 A, or N2 at 2.5 A) the ground state becomes a near-degenerate superposition. The noncontextual model's classical joint value assignment is expected to break down, but the paper does not test this systematically. Without a stretched-bond curve, the CS-VQE method's applicability to the *actually-interesting* strongly-correlated regime is unproven.
next_steps: (1) Extend our H2 script to scan bond lengths 0.5-3.5 A in 0.1 A steps; at each geometry compute FCI, best-CS-VQE at each q, and the q required for 1 mHa accuracy. (2) Plot q_required(R) -- does q grow monotonically with static correlation? (3) Repeat for stretched N2/STO-3G (14 qubits, 10 electrons in 10 orbitals). (4) Correlate q_required with the D1 diagnostic and with |c_HF|^2 in the FCI expansion to give a quantitative predictor of when CS-VQE remains useful.

q: Can a learned model (small GNN over the Pauli-anticommutation graph, or a Transformer over term coefficients) predict a near-optimal noncontextual partition faster than the paper's greedy heuristic, and does the ML-selected partition generalize across molecular families?
basis: Our exhaustive H2 search found partitions the greedy heuristic misses (e.g. the q=0 partition reaching 0.26 mHa uses YXXY, which greedy-by-|coeff| discards). Exhaustive search costs 2^N and is infeasible for N > ~20 terms; a learned selector could amortize the search cost across similar Hamiltonians. Rick's candidate-probe list explicitly names ML-selected partitions as an open direction. No published work as of 2026 does this.
next_steps: (1) Generate a training set of ~10^4 small qubit Hamiltonians (n=4-8) drawn from a mixture of molecular JW mappings (H2, LiH, BeH2, H4 chain at random geometries) plus random symmetric-coefficient Hamiltonians; for each, run exhaustive noncontextual enumeration to label the optimal partition per q. (2) Train a GNN on the anticommutation graph (nodes = terms, edges = anticommutation, node features = |coeff|) to predict per-term nc/c membership. (3) On held-out H2O/STO-3G and NH3/STO-3G, compare (a) exhaustive best, (b) greedy heuristic, (c) GNN-selected partition against FCI. (4) Report qubit-reduction gap and inference wall-time.

q: Is CS-VQE more or less robust to realistic device noise (T1/T2 decoherence, readout error, crosstalk) than full VQE at the same target energy accuracy, once the smaller circuit is actually run on a parameterized ansatz (not just diagonalized classically as in this replication)?
basis: This replication (and the paper's headline sweeps) simulate the quantum correction classically via direct eigen-decomposition of the projected Hamiltonian; sampling noise, ansatz limits, and gate noise are entirely absent. The whole practical case for CS-VQE on near-term hardware rests on the reduced-qubit circuit being noise-robust, but there is no direct experimental or noisy-simulation evidence in the paper.
next_steps: (1) For H2/STO-3G, build a hardware-efficient ansatz on q=1 (CS-VQE) and q=4 (full VQE); use Qiskit's UCC or EfficientSU2 with matched circuit depth per qubit. (2) Simulate with Qiskit Aer's noise model calibrated from a public IBM Falcon backend (T1 ~ 100 us, T2 ~ 80 us, 2q gate error ~ 1e-2). (3) Run 100 VQE optimizations per (ansatz, shots-per-eval in {1024, 8192, 65536}); record mean best energy and its std vs shot budget. (4) Extend to LiH/STO-3G (12 qubits full, ~ 4-6 qubit CS-VQE) to test whether the CS-VQE noise-robustness advantage grows with system size.
